title: Mosaics
objective: After this level you can explain how mosaics are made and where they flourished.
summary: Mosaics are pictures of small closely set tesserae. Greeks invented cut tesserae; Romans laid mosaic floors across the empire, like Pompeii's Alexander Mosaic.

cards.headline: A Pompeii doorway still says "Beware of the dog".
cards.body: At the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, a black dog on a chain is set into the floor in tiny pieces of stone, above the words CAVE CANEM. Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE, and the warning survived. It's a mosaic: a picture you could walk on.

cards.headline: Pictures made of dice
cards.body: A mosaic is built from tesserae: small, closely set pieces of stone, glass, tile or shell. The name is Latin for "cubes" or "dice". The Greeks refined floor pictures made of pebbles, then invented cut tesserae, shaped to fit tightly together. Tighter pieces meant denser, more detailed pictures, the way more pixels make a sharper photo.

cards.headline: The Alexander Mosaic
cards.body: In the House of the Faun, another Pompeii house, lay a floor about 5.8 m wide, made around 100 BCE from more than a million tesserae. It shows Alexander the Great fighting the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus. Scholars believe it's a Roman copy of a lost Greek painting. If so, a great Greek painting survives only as a Roman floor.

cards.headline: Floors of an empire
cards.body: Roman mosaics spread throughout the empire as floor decoration. The same art covered a guard-dog warning at a front door and a great battle in the House of the Faun. Across the empire, Romans walked on pictures.
